title: How to evaluate financial advisors and choose a fee-only planner
description: Understanding the difference between Fiduciaries and Salespeople.
content:
The term 'Financial Advisor' is not strictly regulated in the US. Anyone from a highly trained Certified Financial Planner (CFP) to a life insurance salesman can use the title. This ambiguity costs Americans billions in unnecessary fees and bad products. The most important distinction to understand is how they get paid. Are they paid by *you* to give advice (Fee-Only), or are they paid by *companies* to sell you products (Commission)? This guide gives you the tools to vet an advisor and ensure they are legally obligated to put your interests first.

Key Takeaways

  • The Fiduciary Standard: You must ask: 'Are you a fiduciary 100% of the time?' A fiduciary is legally required to act in your best interest. A broker is only required to sell 'suitable' products.
  • Fee-Only vs. Fee-Based: 'Fee-Only' means they accept NO commissions. 'Fee-Based' means they charge you a fee BUT can also accept commissions. Fee-Only is the gold standard.
  • The 1% AUM Model: Most advisors charge 1% of Assets Under Management. On a $1M portfolio, that is $10,000/year. Ensure you are getting $10k worth of value (tax planning, estate prep), not just investment picking.
  • Credentials Matter: Look for the CFP® (Certified Financial Planner) designation. It requires rigorous education, exams, and experience.

Why It Matters (US Context)

The 'Regulation Best Interest' (Reg BI) passed by the SEC attempted to raise standards for brokers, but loopholes remain. Many 'dual-registered' advisors can switch hats between Fiduciary and Salesperson in the same meeting. Written confirmation of fiduciary status is your best defense.

Compensation Models

How you pay determines what advice you get.

1. Commission-Based (The Salesman)

  • Cost: Free upfront, but hidden costs.
  • Conflict: They sell 'Load' mutual funds (5.75% fee) or Whole Life Insurance because it pays them the highest commission.
  • Verdict: Avoid. You are the product, not the client.

2. AUM (Percentage of Assets)

  • Cost: ~1% of your portfolio annually.
  • Conflict: They are incentivized to gather assets. They might tell you not to pay off your mortgage because that reduces the assets they manage.
  • Verdict: Good for wealthy delegators ($2M+) who want concierge service. Expensive for accumulators.

3. Flat Fee / Hourly (The Consultant)

  • Cost: $2,500 for a plan or $250/hour.
  • Conflict: Minimal. You pay for time/expertise, like a lawyer or CPA.
  • Verdict: Best for most people. You get the roadmap, then implement it yourself at Fidelity/Vanguard.

The Interview Checklist

  1. Check BrokerCheck: Go to FINRA's BrokerCheck website. Type in their name. Look for 'Disclosures'. If they have customer complaints or lawsuits, run.
  2. Ask the 'Hard' Question: "Do you receive any compensation from third parties, mutual fund companies, or insurance providers?" If the answer is anything other than 'No', they are not Fee-Only.
  3. Review the ADV Part 2: This is a required SEC disclosure document. It lists their conflicts of interest in plain English. Read it.
  4. Define Scope: Do you want investment management (trading for you) or financial planning (retirement projections)? Don't pay for management if you just want a plan.

Frequently Asked Questions

Do I need an advisor?

If you have a simple W-2 job and a 401(k), probably not. A Target Date Fund does the investing work. You might need a CPA for taxes, but not a wealth manager.

Is a 'Financial Coach' the same?

No. Coaches focus on budgeting and behavior. They generally cannot give specific investment advice (buying specific stocks) legally. Good for debt problems, not portfolio construction.

What is NAPFA?

The National Association of Personal Financial Advisors. It is a trade group exclusively for Fee-Only fiduciaries. It is a great place to search for a planner.
